prompt: For 0/1 knapsack, ratio-greedy on items (w 1, v 2) and (w 10, v 10) with capacity 10 returns 2, while the optimum is 10. For positive weights and non-negative values, first discard items heavier than capacity. Which simple fix guarantees at least half the optimum when ratio-greedy takes the whole-item prefix up to its first non-fitting item?

options.text: Sort by value instead of ratio
options.explanation: Value-greedy fails too: many light, moderately valuable items can beat one heavy, valuable item that it grabs first.

options.text: Run ratio-greedy twice, the second time on the leftover items
options.explanation: The second pass can't fix a bad first choice: the light item has already used capacity the heavy item needed.

options.text: Use fractional knapsack and round the answer down
options.explanation: Rounding the value doesn't give a feasible set of whole items. You'd still need to decide which fractional item to drop, which is the fix in the correct option.

options.text: Return the better of ratio-greedy and the single most valuable item that fits
options.explanation: Correct. This is a classic 2-approximation (always within a factor of 2): the optimum is at most the greedy prefix plus the next item that didn't fit, so one of the two is at least half the optimum.

workedExample:
1. Why plain ratio-greedy is unbounded: the small item (ratio 2) goes in first, and the big item (ratio 1, value 10) no longer fits. Scale the big item's weight and value and the capacity up together: the big item's ratio stays 1, greedy still returns 2, and the optimum keeps growing. Greedy's share of the optimum tends to zero.
2. Why the fix works: the fractional answer (allowed to take part of an item) is at least the true optimum. It equals greedy's whole-item prefix plus part of the first item that didn't fit, so the optimum is at most the prefix plus that whole next item.
3. That next item fits on its own, so it is worth no more than the best single item. The prefix and the next item are each at most the better of the two candidates, so the optimum is at most twice the better candidate.
4. Here the candidates are 2 (the prefix) and 10 (the big item alone). The better one, 10, is the optimum itself.

An algorithm that isn't exact can still carry a provable guarantee: this one is a 2-approximation.
